packet.headline_seed: Four days of extreme rain killed 7% of world's rarest orangutans, study says
packet.description_seed: Climate change-induced weather events are pushing orangutan populations to extinction, says a study.

what: Four days of extreme rain killed 7% of world's rarest orangutans, study says

clean_source_blocks.text: Climate change-induced weather events are pushing orangutan populations to extinction, says a study.

Four days of extreme rain and landslides in the Indonesian island of Sumatra have pushed the world's most endangered great apes even closer to extinction, says a study. Research suggests that 58 of less than 800 critically endangered Tapanuli orangutans, or around 7% of the total species, were killed as a result of the extreme weather event last November. Those are conservative figures, and do not take into account rain-induced canopy damage or reduced food availability, said the authors of the study published on Wednesday. Cyclone Senyar ravaged Sumatra in late November, killing more than 1,000 people in Southeast Asia's deadliest natural disaster for 2025. The study's findings, said the authors, show that extreme rainfall events can directly threaten the survival of great ape populations.

Critically endangered Tapanuli orangutan population falls after heavy rain and landslides, fuelled by climate crisis, in North Sumatra Extreme rainfall and landslides fuelled by the climate crisis killed 7% of the remaining population of the world’s rarest great ape, a study has found, prompting fears for the species’ survival. The research suggests 58 out of the remaining 800 critically endangered Tapanuli orangutans (Pongo tapanuliensis) were killed after more than 1,000mm (39in) of rain fell over four days in Indonesia’s North Sumatra province in November 2025. This equates to 11% of the local population and 7% of the entire species.

Satellite imagery also revealed that approximately 8,300 hectares (20,510 acres) – 11.7% – of this key forest habitat were wiped out by landslides caused by extreme rainfall. The scientists said human-induced climate change caused by the burning of fossil fuels had increased the rainfall intensity by up to 50%. “The loss of an estimated 58 Tapanuli orangutans to a single climate-induced landslide event is a devastating demographic shock to the world’s rarest great ape,” said Prof Jatna Supriatna, a conservation biologist at Universitas Indonesia. “To prevent the first modern extinction of a great ape species, Indonesia must permanently protect the Batang Toru ecosystem, but our international partners must also meet their global commitments by providing immediate biodiversity-recovery financing.” Previous research has suggested annual losses of 1% of the Tapanuli orangutan population would be sufficient to lead to eventual extinction.

Four days of extreme rain and landslides in the Indonesian island of Sumatra have pushed the world's most endangered great apes even closer to extinction, says a study.

Research suggests that 58 of less than 800 critically endangered Tapanuli orangutans, or around 7% of the total species, were killed as a result of the extreme weather event last November.

Those are conservative figures, and do not take into account rain-induced canopy damage or reduced food availability,  said the authors of the study published on Wednesday.

Cyclone Senyar ravaged Sumatra in late November, killing more than 1,000 people in Southeast Asia's deadliest natural disaster for 2025.

The study's findings, said the authors, show that extreme rainfall events can directly threaten the survival of great ape populations.

Wildlife experts and conservationists had previously observed that, in the wake of the storm, Tapanuli orangutan sightings had dissipated - fuelling speculation that the great apes may have been swept away by floods and landslides.

Professor Erik Meijaard, managing director of Borneo Futures in Brunei and an author of the study published on Wednesday, had told the BBC in December that Cyclone Senyar had likely killed about 35 orangutans – a loss which he said would constitute "a major blow to the population".

Now this comprehensive study has shown the region lost nearly double the number.

Weeks after the cyclone, humanitarian workers told the BBC they found the carcass of what they believed to be a Tapanuli orangutan semi-buried amid debris of mud and logs in Pulo Pakkat village in central Tapanuli district.

"I have seen several dead bodies of humans in the past few days but this was the first dead wildlife," said Deckey Chandra, who was working with a humanitarian team in the area. "They used to come to this place to eat fruits. But now it seems to have become their graveyard."

Meijaard said he had seen photos of the dead orangutan, shared by Chandra.

"What struck me is that all the flesh had been ripped off the face," he said. "If a few hectares of forest comes down in massive landslides, even powerful orangutans are helpless and just get mangled."

"It must have been hellish in the forest at the time."

Researchers noted that Cyclone Senyar was an anomalous event, but that human-induced climate change played a significant role.

[Lähde: The Guardian]
Critically endangered Tapanuli orangutan population falls after heavy rain and landslides, fuelled by climate crisis, in North Sumatra

Extreme rainfall and landslides fuelled by the climate crisis killed 7% of the remaining population of the world’s rarest great ape, a study has found, prompting fears for the species’ survival.

The research suggests 58 out of the remaining 800 critically endangered Tapanuli orangutans (Pongo tapanuliensis) were killed after more than 1,000mm (39in) of rain fell over four days in Indonesia’s North Sumatra province in November 2025. This equates to 11% of the local population and 7% of the entire species.

“It is tragic to lose so many apes in this way. In landscapes where populations are small and fragmented, this type of weather or climate event can have population-level consequences. It is extremely worrying for the future of this ape,” said Prof Serge Wich, a primatologist at Liverpool John Moores University and co-author of the study, published in the journal Current Biology.

The scientists overlaid new analysis of satellite imagery with estimates of ape density to work out the impacts of Cyclone Senyar on the orangutan population in its primary habitat in the West Block of the Batang Toru ecosystem, already threatened by mining, palm oil plantations and a large hydropower project.

Satellite imagery also revealed that approximately 8,300 hectares (20,510 acres) – 11.7% – of this key forest habitat were wiped out by landslides caused by extreme rainfall. The scientists said human-induced climate change caused by the burning of fossil fuels had increased the rainfall intensity by up to 50%.

“The loss of an estimated 58 Tapanuli orangutans to a single climate-induced landslide event is a devastating demographic shock to the world’s rarest great ape,” said Prof Jatna Supriatna, a conservation biologist at Universitas Indonesia. “To prevent the first modern extinction of a great ape species, Indonesia must permanently protect the Batang Toru ecosystem, but our international partners must also meet their global commitments by providing immediate biodiversity-recovery financing.”

Previous research has suggested annual losses of 1% of the Tapanuli orangutan population would be sufficient to lead to eventual extinction.

payload.title: Tutkimus: Neljän päivän rankkasateet tappoivat arviolta seitsemän prosenttia maailman harvinaisimmista orankeista
payload.summary: Pohjois-Sumatralla marraskuussa 2025 sattunut äärimmäinen sade- ja maanvyörytapahtuma surmasi tutkimuksen mukaan arviolta 58 tapanulinorankia. Määrä vastaa noin seitsemää prosenttia koko äärimmäisen uhanalaisesta lajista.
payload.content:
Pohjois-Sumatralla Indonesiassa marraskuussa 2025 koettu neljän päivän äärimmäinen sadejakso ja sitä seuranneet maanvyöryt tappoivat tutkimuksen mukaan arviolta 58 tapanulinorankia. Se on noin seitsemän prosenttia koko lajista, jota on jäljellä alle 800 yksilöä, ja tutkijat pitävät tapahtumaa vakavana iskuna maailman harvinaisimmalle ihmisapinalle.

## Harvinainen ihmisapina menetti suuren osan kannastaan

Tapanulinoranki (Pongo tapanuliensis) on äärimmäisen uhanalainen laji. Tutkimuksen mukaan Pohjois-Sumatralla satoi neljän päivän aikana yli 1 000 millimetriä, mikä johti tuhoisiin maanvyöryihin lajin keskeisellä elinalueella.

Arvioitu 58 yksilön menetys vastaa 11:tä prosenttia paikallisesta kannasta ja seitsemää prosenttia koko lajista. Tutkijoiden mukaan luku on varovainen arvio, sillä se ei sisällä sateiden aiheuttamia latvusvaurioita tai ravinnon saatavuuden heikkenemistä.

Satelliittikuvat osoittivat, että noin 8 300 hehtaaria tärkeää metsäelinympäristöä tuhoutui maanvyöryissä. Tämä vastaa 11,7:ää prosenttia kyseisestä keskeisestä metsäalueesta.

## Ilmastonmuutos lisäsi sateen voimakkuutta

Tutkijoiden mukaan fossiilisten polttoaineiden poltosta johtuva ihmisen aiheuttama ilmastonmuutos lisäsi sateen voimakkuutta jopa 50 prosentilla. Tutkimuksen tekijät katsovat havaintojen osoittavan, että äärimmäiset sadetapahtumat voivat uhata suoraan ihmisapinoiden selviytymistä.

Marraskuun lopulla Sumatraa koetellut Senyar-sykloni oli osa laajaa luonnonkatastrofia, jossa kuoli yli 1 000 ihmistä Kaakkois-Aasiassa. Samalla tapahtuma aiheutti tutkijoiden mukaan vakavan iskun tapanulinorankien jo valmiiksi pienelle kannalle.

## Tutkijat vaativat suojelutoimia

Universitas Indonesian luonnonsuojelubiologi Jatna Supriatna kuvasi 58 yksilön menetystä tuhoisaksi demografiseksi iskuksi maailman harvinaisimmalle ihmisapinalle. Hän vaati Batang Torun ekosysteemin pysyvää suojelua sekä kansainvälistä rahoitusta luonnon monimuotoisuuden elvyttämiseen.

Aiemman tutkimuksen mukaan jo yhden prosentin vuotuinen menetys tapanulinorankien kannasta voisi riittää viemään lajin ajan myötä kohti sukupuuttoa. Tutkimuksen mukaan nyt havaittu menetys oli moninkertainen tähän rajaan verrattuna yhdessä ainoassa sää- ja maanvyörytapahtumassa.
summary_bullets: Tutkimuksen mukaan 58 tapanulinorankia kuoli Pohjois-Sumatran rankkasateiden ja maanvyöryjen seurauksena.
Menetys vastaa noin seitsemää prosenttia koko äärimmäisen uhanalaisesta lajista.
Satelliittikuvat osoittivat, että noin 8 300 hehtaaria keskeistä metsäelinympäristöä tuhoutui.
